title: Install Google Antigravity and say hello
summary: Start with Google’s desktop app. You can have a first conversation before choosing a folder or writing code.
where: Windows 10 (64-bit) or Windows 11, or macOS 13 or later on Apple Silicon or 64-bit Intel, with internet and a Google account. An iPad can display the guide while you follow along on the computer.
Use the Google Antigravity App installer. Google also offers an IDE, a separate editor, and a CLI for typed commands.

actions.title: Choose the desktop app
actions.do: Open antigravity.google/download on the computer and select the Antigravity App for your operating system.
actions.see: The download should be offered by Google on its Antigravity site.
actions.stuck: If the instructions begin with a command to paste, switch from CLI to the App download.

actions.title: Open the installer
actions.do: On Windows open the downloaded installer from Downloads. On Mac open the downloaded disk image and follow its instruction to place the app in Applications.
actions.see: Google Antigravity becomes available from Start or Applications.
actions.stuck: Choose the matching Windows architecture or Mac processor build if the installer reports incompatibility.

actions.title: Sign in
actions.do: Launch Antigravity and complete its Google sign-in in the browser. Return to the app.
actions.see: Some accounts see a work-role question; the Software Engineering option gives a useful layout for these lessons.
actions.stuck: Use Skip if the onboarding version offers it and you are unsure which role fits.

actions.title: Ask one small question
actions.do: At Home, type “What is 7 plus 5? Answer with just the number.” Send it.
actions.see: The reply should contain 12. This exercise uses no files.
actions.stuck: If the app asks you for a project before showing chat, choose a new empty folder using the next lesson.

title: Give the agent one practice folder
summary: A project tells Antigravity which folders belong to a task. A plain folder on your computer is enough for this exercise.
where: Windows or Mac, Antigravity App and an empty folder named AI Practice. No GitHub account is required for a local folder.

actions.title: Make the folder
actions.do: Open File Explorer on Windows or Finder on Mac. In Documents use New Folder and name it AI Practice.
actions.see: The folder opens and has no documents in it yet.
actions.stuck: If you already started with a folder from another lesson, make a fresh folder with a slightly different name.

actions.title: Create a project
actions.do: In Antigravity click the folder-with-plus New Project icon in the left sidebar, choose Add Folder and select AI Practice. Click Create.
actions.see: The conversation can now refer to this project and its selected folder.
actions.stuck: A composer labeled No Project is still at Home. Select the project from the sidebar.

actions.title: Give the first file instruction
actions.do: Type “Create a plain text file named welcome.txt in this folder. Its only line should be Welcome aboard.” Press Enter.
actions.see: In the engineering layout, choose Local mode if the app asks where to run.
actions.stuck: If a worktree is offered, use Local for this plain-folder exercise. A worktree is a separate Git checkout.

actions.title: Open the result yourself
actions.do: Return to the AI Practice folder in Finder or File Explorer and open welcome.txt.
actions.see: It contains Welcome aboard. You can now point to the result outside the conversation.
actions.stuck: If the file is missing, ask Antigravity which folder and filename it used, then compare with your project.

roles: Practice on a sample runbook file.
Create a text file for a sample book.

title: Read a plan before requesting edits
summary: A plan is a proposed sequence of work. Read and revise it before asking the agent to carry it out.
where: Antigravity desktop app on Windows or Mac, online, with an empty practice project open.

actions.title: Request the plan
actions.do: In the project conversation type “/plan Make a one-page packing list with checkboxes for Passport and Charger. Show me the plan before editing files.”
actions.see: A planning reply can include an Implementation Plan card.
actions.stuck: If the command menu pops up, select Plan and enter the rest as your description.

actions.title: Read the proposal
actions.do: Select the plan card to open it in the side panel. Find the proposed file and two labels.
actions.see: The plan describes what the agent intends to build.
actions.stuck: If it only discusses broad goals, ask for the filename, visible labels and a test you can perform.

actions.title: Change one requirement
actions.do: Ask for a third checkbox called Earplugs before starting. Use a comment on the plan or the main conversation.
actions.see: The revised plan includes three items.
actions.stuck: If it begins implementing early, tell it to pause edits and restate the three agreed labels.

actions.title: Carry it out
actions.do: Choose Proceed when offered, or tell the conversation to implement the revised plan. Open the resulting HTML file in your browser.
actions.see: You can check each of the three labeled boxes independently.
actions.stuck: If you see the source as text, use your browser’s Open File command on the .html file.

roles: Plan a small form before building it.

title: Find the exact line Antigravity changed
summary: A diff is a before-and-after view of a file. Use it to check a correction before moving on.
where: Antigravity App online in a practice project on Windows or Mac. The Agent Edits view can show changes made in a conversation.

actions.title: Create the original
actions.do: Ask the project agent to create a file called sign.txt with two lines, Harbor Notes and Dock 3. Open the file and confirm the original.
actions.see: You have a visible baseline on your computer.
actions.stuck: If it put both items on one line, ask it to fix that before the next instruction.

actions.title: Request a single change
actions.do: Send “Change Dock 3 to Dock 4 in sign.txt. Leave the title alone.”
actions.see: The agent reports the file it edited.
actions.stuck: If it creates a copy, ask it to revise the original sign.txt in your selected project.

actions.title: Open Review
actions.do: In the conversation’s Overview panel click Review. If the panel is hidden, use Toggle Overview Panel at the top right. Select Agent Edits and sign.txt.
actions.see: The file and its changes appear beside the conversation.
actions.stuck: A file created during this conversation may appear entirely new. Use the most recent turn’s changes or compare its final lines with your baseline.

actions.title: Leave precise feedback
actions.do: Select the relevant line for a review comment if available, or type “Change Dock 4 to Dock 5 on the second line.” Check sign.txt again.
actions.see: The final lines are Harbor Notes and Dock 5.
actions.stuck: If you see an earlier version in a text editor, reload the file from disk.

roles: Check a title edit in a book.

title: Open Google AI Studio and run a first prompt
summary: AI Studio is Google’s online workbench for trying models. Playground is where you type and run an experiment.
where: Use a browser on a Mac or Windows PC. On iPad try Safari and rotate to landscape for more room; a desktop is easier for the settings panel.
AI Studio documents access for users 18 and older in supported regions. Your organization may restrict it.

actions.title: Open the website
actions.do: Type aistudio.google.com into the address bar, then use your eligible Google account to sign in.
actions.see: A Google AI Studio home page or Playground opens.
actions.stuck: If you see a general Gemini chat, check that the address starts with aistudio.google.com.

actions.title: Find Playground
actions.do: Open Playground from the navigation if a blank chat prompt has not already opened. Choose an available text model.
actions.see: You should see a text box and a Run control.
actions.stuck: A work window showing app source and a preview belongs to Build. Open Playground for this lesson.

actions.title: Send a prompt
actions.do: Type “A card costs 4 dollars. I buy two. Reply with the total in dollars.” Click Run.
actions.see: The answer is 8 dollars.
actions.stuck: If Studio says the selected model requires billing, choose an available model that your account already supports.

actions.title: Run a changed example
actions.do: Open a fresh Playground prompt and ask the same question with three cards.
actions.see: The result changes to 12 dollars. You have repeated the experiment with one input changed.
actions.stuck: If it still says 8, reread the submitted message and confirm the quantity actually changed.

roles: Test wording for a sample support response.
Try extracting a date from an invented notice.
sources: Google · supported regions and age requirements

title: Give a Playground chat a standing rule
summary: System Instructions hold the rule for the conversation. The user message supplies an example for that rule to process.
where: Google AI Studio Playground in an online desktop browser. The same controls can be easier to find in iPad landscape.

actions.title: Open the controls
actions.do: In a new Playground chat click Run settings, the tuning-controls icon at the top right. Find System Instructions.
actions.see: The instruction editor is separate from the ordinary text box.
actions.stuck: If you only see a build preview, switch to Playground and start a text prompt.

actions.title: Set a rule
actions.do: In System Instructions enter “Answer with the color word only. If no color is stated, answer UNKNOWN.”
actions.see: The rule stays available while this prompt is open.
actions.stuck: If you accidentally sent it as a chat message, copy it into System Instructions and start the example again.

actions.title: Try a positive input
actions.do: In the ordinary text box type “The ticket is blue.” Click Run.
actions.see: The intended result is blue, with no sentence around it.
actions.stuck: If the answer adds an explanation, ask it to follow the output rule and check which field contains that rule.

actions.title: Try a missing input
actions.do: In the same chat send “The next ticket has no printed color.”
actions.see: The expected result is UNKNOWN. The earlier blue ticket supplies no color for this new one.
actions.stuck: If the previous color carries over, add “Treat each ticket independently” to the instruction and retest both tickets.

roles: Set the rules for a word-game answer.

title: Build a two-button score counter in a browser
summary: Build turns a description into an app you can try in a preview. This practice app only needs a number and two buttons.
where: Open aistudio.google.com/apps on Mac or Windows while online. The wider desktop view is helpful for seeing chat and preview together.

actions.title: Open Build
actions.do: Visit Google AI Studio and open Build, or go directly to aistudio.google.com/apps. Start a new app from a prompt.
actions.see: A box invites you to describe what to build.
actions.stuck: If you have Run settings for a chat and no app preview, choose Build in the navigation.

actions.title: Describe the counter
actions.do: Enter “Make a browser score counter. Start at zero. Add one adds 1; Reset returns to zero. Show the number in large type. No account or database.” Submit the prompt.
actions.see: The builder prepares files and displays an interactive preview.
actions.stuck: Give it time to finish. If the preview reports an error, copy the visible error into the build conversation and ask for a repair.

actions.title: Use the preview
actions.do: Click Add one twice and Reset once in the running app.
actions.see: The values progress from 0 to 1 to 2, then back to 0.
actions.stuck: If clicking only selects an element for editing, switch back to interacting with the live preview.

actions.title: Revise and retest
actions.do: Ask the builder to add a Subtract one button that can reach negative scores. At zero, click it once.
actions.see: The counter shows −1, and Reset returns it to 0.
actions.stuck: A floor of zero indicates that the requested negative-score behavior still needs correcting.

roles: Build a scoreboard for a card game.

title: Start with Gemini on an iPad, Mac or PC
summary: A chat is a conversation in which you type a question and can refer back to its answer. Try one with numbers you can check.
where: On iPad use the Google Gemini app published by Google, or visit gemini.google.com in Safari. On Windows or Mac the website is enough.

actions.title: Open the right product
actions.do: On iPad, open the App Store and search for Google Gemini. Check the publisher, then choose Get or Open. On a computer visit gemini.google.com.
actions.see: The Gemini home screen has a box for a question.
actions.stuck: If you want to skip installing an app, use the official website instead.

actions.title: Choose the account
actions.do: Sign in if prompted and start a new chat. Check the account shown under the profile picture.
actions.see: An empty chat opens without earlier messages.
actions.stuck: If the screen shows workspace policies or features you did not expect, check whether you selected a work or personal account.

actions.title: Try a small fact pattern
actions.do: Enter “I packed two red shirts and one blue shirt. How many shirts did I pack? Use only these facts.” Send the message.
actions.see: The expected answer is three shirts.
actions.stuck: If dictation changed the words, read your submitted message and type a correction.

actions.title: Ask a follow-up
actions.do: In the same chat type “I remove one red shirt. How many red and blue shirts remain?”
actions.see: One red and one blue shirt remain. The second question relied on the first.
actions.stuck: If you opened a new chat, re-enter the original quantities so it has the starting facts.

roles: Practise summarizing a fictional support note.
Outline a feature on your iPad.

title: Find Tasks, formerly Gemini Spark
summary: A task can carry out several steps and produce a file. The first exercise uses a made-up schedule so no connected accounts are needed.
where: Use the Gemini mobile app or gemini.google.com while online. Access depends on age, account, region and rollout.
Look for Task above the message box. Older guides may call the same capability Spark.

actions.title: Choose Task
actions.do: Open a new Gemini thread and select Task above the text box. Look at its model menu and leave the default selection.
actions.see: The composer is set for a task.
actions.stuck: If Task is missing, consult the linked eligibility page. You can practise the schedule prompt in Chat, but a chat answer cannot demonstrate background task progress.

actions.title: Give a bounded job
actions.do: Enter “Using only this information, make a one-page text packing schedule. Dock opens 08:00. Ferry boards 09:15. Leave home 30 minutes before the dock opens. Put events in order.” Submit.
actions.see: A new task thread appears with progress or an initial reply.
actions.stuck: If Gemini offers to search email or a calendar, clarify that every required fact is in the request.

actions.title: Inspect progress
actions.do: Open the task thread from Menu and tap its progress chip or Task progress at the top.
actions.see: You can see the work or status associated with this thread.
actions.stuck: If it has finished already, open the result in the same thread and inspect its time ordering.

actions.title: Read the result
actions.do: Open the text or file it produced. Compare all three times against the request.
actions.see: Leave at 07:30, arrive for the dock opening at 08:00, and board at 09:15.
actions.stuck: If the departure time is 08:45, ask which time the thirty minutes was subtracted from.

roles: Prepare an itinerary for a personal travel app.
sources: Google · create tasks on iPhone and iPad
Google · Tasks in Gemini, formerly Spark

title: Open Deep Research and inspect one citation
summary: Deep Research prepares a plan and then gathers sources. You control the question and can check the evidence behind an answer.
where: Use Gemini online on a Mac, PC or iPad with Deep Research available to your account. Public sources are sufficient.

actions.title: Select the research tool
actions.do: Open a new Gemini chat. On iPad tap Add files or the tools menu beside the text box, then choose Deep Research.
actions.see: Deep Research is selected for the next request.
actions.stuck: On a computer look in the tools menu. If the option is unavailable, check your plan and usage rather than waiting for ordinary chat to become research.

actions.title: Request one comparison
actions.do: Enter “Using only official public sources, compare how NASA and ESA describe the Hubble Space Telescope. Give one shared fact and a source from each agency.” Submit.
actions.see: Gemini shows a proposed plan for a report.
actions.stuck: If it plans a general history, use Edit plan and narrow it to one fact both agencies support.

actions.title: Begin the work
actions.do: Choose Start research and return to the thread when the report is ready. Select Open to read it.
actions.see: The report presents an answer with sources.
actions.stuck: If the thread is still displaying a plan, confirm that you selected Start research after editing it.

actions.title: Follow the evidence
actions.do: Open one citation from each agency and find the sentence that supports your chosen shared fact.
actions.see: You can point to the fact on both original pages.
actions.stuck: If one page merely mentions Hubble, ask for a citation supporting the exact claim and verify the replacement.

roles: Find sources for a trivia book.
sources: Google · Deep Research on iPhone and iPad

title: Build a notebook from two short notes
summary: Give Gemini Notebook, formerly NotebookLM, two sources. Find out which one it used to answer a question.
where: On iPad, open the Gemini Notebook app if available. On desktop, open the Google notebook experience. Use an eligible account and a fresh notebook.

actions.title: Create the notebook
actions.do: Open the notebook list. Choose Create new or New notebook. Name it Ferry Day. A notebook is a place to gather material you want the helper to read together.
actions.see: The new notebook has a name and an area for its sources. Each source is a separate item.
actions.stuck: If Gemini opens in an ordinary chat, switch to the notebook area or open the standalone Gemini Notebook service.

actions.title: Add two sources
actions.do: Add these as two separate pasted notes or plain-text files. Call one Schedule and give it “Meet at Pier 6 at 9:15.” Call the other Packing and give it “Bring a hat and a notebook.”
actions.see: The source list has two entries. Open each one and check its text before asking anything.
actions.stuck: If pasted text is unavailable on your device, save two small text files and use the upload option.

actions.title: Follow the evidence
actions.do: Ask “Which pier, and what should I bring? Show the source for each answer.” Open a citation or source reference beside the answer.
actions.see: The pier comes from Schedule. The hat and notebook come from Packing. You can see why two sources were useful.
actions.stuck: If the reply mixes them up, ask one question about the pier and another about the packing list.

actions.title: Find a limit
actions.do: Ask “What does the ticket cost?” Look through both sources for a price. Say what you would need to add to answer that question.
actions.see: Neither note includes a price. A fare notice would make a useful third source.
actions.stuck: If an amount appears anyway, ask for the exact passage that gives it. Keep the price unknown until the passage actually exists.

roles: Compare two public reference notes when learning a reporting command.
Keep a sample meeting agenda and its notes as separate sources.
Ground your app’s help text in the actual feature list.
